newsitem.title: GERMANY: LIFFE official explains sugar contract changes.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE official explains sugar contract changes.

text.p: Changes to the No.5 white sugar contract on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) are based on careful research, said Clive Furness, LIFFE's director of commodity products.
"We based the changes on input from 50 to 60 companies worldwide," he told Reuters during a promotional visit here.
"We feel very strongly we have a contract that is sound and in its construction we took what is good and made it better."
"The market also feels we've found a central path."
The changes, which were announced on April 11, will affect the contract from the August 1998 delivery month onwards.

Furness rejected criticism from some market quarters that the ruling reducing the maximum ICUMSA colour for non-EU ports from 60 units to 45 for delivery against the contract would favour EU origin sugar.
"The aim was to standardise the practice, it was never going to be satisfying to all," he said.
This aim was also reflected in the change to the minimum loading rate for sugars delivered in fulfilment of delivery obligations to 1,000 tonnes a day from 750 tonnes, he said.
LIFFE believed this reflected the practice in modern ports.
He said delivery ports had been selected on the basis of commercial importance and functionality in order to meet the requirements of a fob-based contract.
The Guatemalan port of Quetzal would be included from August 1998, but South Africa so far was not represented.
Furness said the introduction of a differential for sugar delivered in polypropylene (PP) bags was based on statistics showing some 85 percent of all sugar now arrived that way.
The differential for PP bags would be constantly monitored and adjusted.
LIFFE claims to account for 75-80 percent of global white sugar futures trading.
The exchange was also assessing very closely its robusta coffee contract with a view to improving the effectiveness of lot sizes and implied costs of trading, but it was "early days".
